t:
Chapter 44 of title 18, United States Code, is amended—
    (1) in section 926B—
        (A) in subsection (c)(1), by inserting “or apprehension under section 807(b) of title 10, United States Code (article 7(b) of the Uniform Code of Military Justice)” after “arrest”; 
        (B) in subsection (d), by striking “as a law enforcement officer” and inserting “that identifies the employee as a police officer or law enforcement officer of the agency”; and 
        (C) in subsection (f), by inserting “or apprehension under section 807(b) of title 10, United States Code (article 7(b) of the Uniform Code of Military Justice)” after “arrest”; and  
    (2) in section 926C—
        (A) in subsection (c)(2), by inserting “or apprehension under section 807(b) of title 10, United States Code (article 7(b) of the Uniform Code of Military Justice)” after “arrest”; and 
        (B) in subsection (d)—
            (i) in paragraph (1), by striking “that indicates” and inserting “that identifies the person as having been employed as a police officer or law enforcement officer and indicates”; and 
            (ii) in paragraph (2)(A), by inserting “that identifies the person as having been employed as a police officer or law enforcement officer” after “officer”.

fable.w: This section only makes technical amendments to 18 U.S.C. 926B and 926C, adding military apprehension authority under 10 U.S.C. 807(b) and clarifying the identification that qualified and retired law enforcement officers must carry. There is no tempting participation reading: nothing provides for consultation, public comment, rulemaking, an advisory body, a hearing, or a right to sue involving anyone outside the federal government. It changes definitions and eligibility criteria and does not set up any process for outside input into a federal decision.

opus.w: This section only makes technical changes to the definitions and identification requirements for concealed carry by current and retired officers in 18 U.S.C. 926B and 926C. It sets up no comment period, rulemaking, hearing, advisory body, consultation with outside groups, or right to sue. Mentions of arrest, apprehension, or agency ID describe who qualifies. They do not bring anyone outside the federal government into a federal decision.
opus.s: in subsection (d), by striking “as a law enforcement officer” and inserting “that identifies the employee as a police officer or law enforcement officer of the agency”
opus.b:
1. **Reasoning.** One could be tempted to read the references to "apprehension under... the Uniform Code of Military Justice" and to agency-issued identification as some kind of process involving outside parties. That reading fails. These are technical wording changes to 18 U.S.C. 926B and 926C, which allow current and retired law enforcement officers to carry concealed firearms. They change definitions and what an ID card must say. Nothing requires the federal government to consult, hold hearings, take comments, write rules, set up an advisory body, or give anyone a right to sue before it decides something.

2. **Label.**

qwen_chat.w: This section consists entirely of technical amendments to existing statutes regarding law enforcement identification and arrest powers. It does not create any advisory committees, public comment periods, or consultation requirements with outside parties. All actors mentioned (law enforcement officers, agencies) are part of the government or regulated entities, but the text does not describe a participatory decision-making process involving outsiders.
qwen_chat.s: Chapter 44 of title 18, United States Code, is amended— (1) in section 926B— (A) in subsection (c)(1), by inserting “or apprehension under section 807(b) of title 10, United States Code (article 7(b) of the Uniform Code of Military Justice)” after “arrest”; (B) in subsection (d), by striking “as a law enforcement officer” and inserting “that identifies the employee as a police officer or law enforcement officer of the agency”; and (C) in subsection (f), by inserting “or apprehension under section 807(b) of title 10, United States Code (article 7(b) of the Uniform Code of Military Justice)” after “arrest”; and (2) in section 926C— (A) in subsection (c)(2), by inserting “or apprehension under section 807(b) of title 10, United States Code (article 7(b) of the Uniform Code of Military Justice)” after “arrest”; and (B) in subsection (d)— (i) in paragraph (1), by striking “that indicates” and inserting “that identifies the person as having been employed as a police officer or law enforcement officer and indicates”; and (ii) in paragraph (2)(A), by inserting “that identifies the person as having been employed as a police officer or law enforcement officer” after “officer”.
qwen_chat.b: Tempting-but-wrong reading: One might argue that because the text amends laws regarding law enforcement officers, it involves public participation. However, the text itself only describes technical amendments to statutory language regarding identification cards and arrest powers. It does not establish any process for consulting with the public, states, or other outside entities. The actors involved are federal agencies and officers (inside the government).
